lessonTitle: Heat and Other Work Modes: Energy in Transit

blocks.text: An electric motor on a test bench drives a pump through a shaft, and the same motor casing is hot to the touch. One energy stream leaves the motor shaft as work and another leaves its casing as heat. Telling these two apart, and putting numbers on each, is the first step in every energy balance.

blocks.markdown: Energy crosses the boundary of a closed system in only two ways: as **heat** or as **work**. Both are energy in transit: neither is stored by the system, and both vanish once the transfer is over. The difference lies in what drives the transfer.

blocks.title: Heat and work
blocks.text: Heat $Q$ (kJ) is energy transferred across a boundary because of a temperature difference. Work $W$ (kJ) is energy transferred by any other cause: a force acting through a distance, a torque turning through an angle, or an electric potential moving charge. Rates are $\dot Q$ and $\dot W$ in kW.

rows: Hot to cold only (without a device)
Conduction through a wall, convection, radiation
Boundary motion, rotating shaft, electrical current, stretching a spring
blocks.caption: Heat and work compared

blocks.markdown: Three work modes appear constantly in this course. **Boundary work** is covered in the previous unit. **Shaft work** arises when a rotating shaft crosses the boundary, as in a turbine, compressor or stirrer. **Electrical work** arises when current flows through the boundary under a voltage, as in a heater element or battery. Shaft work is torque times angle turned, so its rate is torque times angular speed.

blocks.caption: $T$ torque (N m), $\omega$ angular speed (rad/s), $n$ rotational speed (rev/min); the result is in watts
Voltage V (volts) times current I (amperes) gives watts; electrical work over time t is $W_{el}=VIt$

blocks.title: Shaft power of a motor
blocks.prompt: A motor shaft delivers a torque of 150 N m at 1450 rev/min. Find the shaft power in kW.

steps.text: Multiply by torque and convert W to kW.

blocks.answer: The shaft power is about 22.8 kW.

blocks.caption: $W$ is the net work done by the system summed over all modes

blocks.title: Heat transfer from energy change and work
blocks.prompt: A gas in a cylinder gains 30 kJ of internal energy while doing 12 kJ of boundary work on a piston. Find the heat transfer.

steps.text: Write the first law solved for heat.
Substitute with W positive because it is done by the gas.

blocks.answer: Q = 42 kJ, positive, so 42 kJ of heat flows into the gas.

blocks.title: Electrical heater energy
blocks.prompt: A 2 kW resistance heater is on for 5 minutes. How much electrical energy crosses a boundary that encloses the heater and its cable?

steps.text: Power times time with time in seconds.

steps.latex: W_{el}=600\ \text{kJ}\ (\text{done on the system, so}\ W=-600\ \text{kJ})

blocks.answer: 600 kJ of electrical work is done on the system.

blocks.title: Boundary choice decides the label
blocks.text: Whether an energy transfer is heat or work depends on where the boundary is drawn. If the system is a tank of water, current heating a resistor immersed in it counts as heat from the resistor. If the boundary includes the resistor, the same flow is electrical work.

blocks.title: Stirring is work
blocks.text: Friction and stirring raise temperature but are work, not heat, because no temperature difference drives them. An insulated tank with a stirrer still receives energy.

points: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; work is energy transfer by force, torque or voltage; neither is a property.
Shaft power is torque times angular speed, 2 pi n T/60 for n in rev/min, and electrical power is VI.
For a closed system Q = Delta U + W, using the sign convention heat in and work out positive.
The classification of a transfer depends on the choice of system boundary.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes heat from work?

options.text: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, work by any other driving cause
Heat is stored in a body, work is not
Work always raises temperature, heat never does
Heat can only be transferred in a vacuum

questions.correctOptionText: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, work by any other driving cause

distractorRationale.b: Neither is stored; both are energy in transit.
distractorRationale.c: Heat may or may not change temperature; work can raise it too.
distractorRationale.d: Heat transfers by conduction, convection and radiation in many media.

questions.explanation: Heat is defined by its driving cause, a temperature difference, while work arises from forces, torques or voltages. Both are boundary phenomena rather than stored quantities.

questions.stem: A paddle wheel stirs the water in a rigid, perfectly insulated tank and the water temperature rises. What kind of energy transfer is this for a system consisting of the water?

options.text: Work, because no temperature difference drives the transfer
Neither, because the tank is insulated
Both heat and work in equal amounts

questions.correctOptionText: Work, because no temperature difference drives the transfer

distractorRationale.a: Temperature increase alone does not define heat.
distractorRationale.c: Insulation stops heat, not shaft work.
distractorRationale.d: Only shaft work crosses the boundary.

questions.explanation: The paddle shaft exerts a torque through an angle, so energy crosses the boundary as shaft work. There is no temperature difference to drive heat, and the work shows up as an increase in internal energy.

questions.stem: A shaft transmits torque T in N m at speed n in rev/min. Which expression gives the power in watts?

distractorRationale.a: Missing the unit conversion from rev/min to rad/s.
distractorRationale.b: Divides by speed instead of multiplying.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong direction of the 2 pi factor.

questions.explanation: Power is torque times angular speed, and omega = 2 pi n/60 in rad/s when n is in rev/min. The product 2 pi n T/60 is in newton-metres per second, which are watts.

questions.stem: A gas in a closed cylinder loses 10 kJ of internal energy while doing 25 kJ of work on the surroundings. What is the heat transfer?

distractorRationale.a: Adds both with the wrong signs.
distractorRationale.d: Treats the internal energy loss as a gain.

questions.explanation: Using Q = delta U + W with delta U = -10 kJ and W = +25 kJ gives Q = +15 kJ. The gas must take in 15 kJ of heat to supply work beyond its stored energy loss.

questions.stem: A resistor sits in a tank of water inside an insulated container, powered by an external supply. Taking the system as the water only, how is the energy from the resistor classified?

options.text: Heat, because it crosses the water boundary because of a temperature difference

questions.correctOptionText: Heat, because it crosses the water boundary because of a temperature difference

distractorRationale.a: This is true only if the resistor is inside the boundary.
distractorRationale.c: The water boundary does not move.
distractorRationale.d: It can be classified once the boundary is defined.

questions.explanation: For a boundary drawn around the water, energy arrives from the hotter resistor by a temperature difference, so it is heat. With the resistor inside the boundary, the same transfer would be electrical work, so the label depends on the chosen system.

questions.stem: A shaft transmits a torque of 85 N m at 3000 rev/min. Find the shaft power in kW.
questions.explanation: The angular speed is 2 pi x 3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s. Then P = 85 x 314.16 = 26704 W = 26.70 kW.

questions.stem: A turbine delivers 12 kW of shaft power while rotating at 200 rad/s. Find the torque on the shaft in N m.
questions.explanation: Power equals torque times angular speed, so T = P/omega = 12000/200 = 60 N m. Power must be converted from kW to W for the units to match.

questions.stem: A gas in a cylinder is stirred by a paddle that does 15 kJ of work on it while the gas does 20 kJ of work on a piston. Its internal energy falls by 8 kJ. Find the heat transfer in kJ (heat into the system positive).
questions.explanation: The net work done by the gas is 20 - 15 = 5 kJ. Then Q = delta U + W = -8 + 5 = -3 kJ, so 3 kJ of heat leaves the gas.

questions.stem: A stirrer in a rigid, perfectly insulated tank of liquid turns at 120 rev/min with a steady torque of 4 N m for 10 minutes. Find the work done on the liquid, state the heat transfer and the change in internal energy of the liquid, and explain why this process counts as work not heat.
markingGuide: Energy over 600 s = 30.2 kJ done on the liquid
Rigid tank means no boundary work and insulated means Q = 0, so Delta U = +30.2 kJ
No temperature difference drives the transfer, only a torque turning through an angle, so it is work
questions.explanation: The work over ten minutes is 30.2 kJ, all of which appears as internal energy since Q = 0 and there is no boundary work. It is classed as work because a torque acting through an angle, not a temperature difference, drives it.

questions.stem: Give three differences or similarities between heat and work as modes of energy transfer, and explain why neither is a property of a system.
markingGuide: Both are energy in transit crossing the boundary
Heat is driven by temperature difference, work by force, torque or voltage
Both depend on the path, not only on end states
So neither can be written as a function of state and they are not properties
Differences in sign convention: Q into system positive, W by system positive
questions.explanation: Both heat and work exist only during a process, so they cannot be assigned to a state. The distinction rests on the driving cause, and the amounts depend on the path between the end states.
